Case study · UX research

UTS Mobile App: redesigning ticket booking

Indian Railways passengers use UTS to book unreserved tickets, often on the platform and in a hurry. I mapped the booking journey, found where it broke down, and redesigned it from 8 steps to 5.

RoleUX research & UI design
ScopeBooking journey
ToolsFigma
Outcome8 → 5 steps (−37%)
The problem

Booking was slow and confusing for daily commuters

Too many steps8 steps to buy one ticket, which is a lot for someone booking every day.
Features were hard to findWeak information hierarchy buried key features.
No clear primary actionThe most important actions didn't stand out, so people hesitated.
Unnecessary screensRedundant screens and loading slowed every booking.
The redesign

A five-step booking flow

  1. STEP 1Select journey type
  2. STEP 2Choose origin & destination
  3. STEP 3Pick ticket type & passengers
  4. STEP 4Review journey details
  5. STEP 5Confirm & get ticket
Impact

Before vs after

Old flow
8steps
New flow
5steps
37% fewer stepsFrom 8 steps down to 5
Clearer navigationA rebuilt information hierarchy
Faster bookingRedundant screens removed
Better clarityPrimary actions stand out

Tip for Spruha: add how you found these problems (e.g. "interviewed N commuters", "timed 5 bookings") and one usability result for the new flow. That turns this from a redesign into a research case study.

Case study · Design operations

Design–Developer Collaboration

Good designs lose accuracy in the build when handoffs are unclear, specs go missing, and design and engineering stop talking. I set up a structured workflow for build validation, UI QA and issue tracking so the design intent survives to release.

RoleUX project manager
FocusDesign fidelity
ToolsCassini, Figma
TeamsDesign + Engineering
The challenge

What was going wrong

Builds didn't match designsUI inconsistencies between design files and product builds.
Specs were misreadDesign specifications were misinterpreted during implementation.
Bugs were caught lateDesign-related bugs surfaced only at the end of the cycle.
Too much back-and-forthDesigners and developers kept going round in circles on the same issues.
My approach

A four-part framework

Build & UAT validationTested every UAT build against the specs for layout, typography, spacing and interactions.
Bug tracking in CassiniLogged layout inconsistencies, missing components and interaction errors, and tracked each one until it was fixed.
Bridging design & engineeringClarified design intent with both teams so gaps were closed quickly.
Continuous design QAMoved design validation into the development cycle instead of leaving it for final QA.
Workflow

The delivery pipeline

Design delivery Developer build UAT build testing Cassini bug report Design–dev alignment Release
Impact

Results

Higher build accuracyBuilds matched the designs more closely
Issues caught earlierUI bugs found during development
Fewer gapsLess design–dev miscommunication
Smoother releasesMore efficient QA and releases

Tip for Spruha: if the 25% turnaround gain and 30% consistency gain from your Canvs role came from this workflow, add them here. Numbers make this case much stronger.

Takeaway

By giving both teams one consistent way to review builds and log UI issues, I helped set up a lasting collaboration framework, so the team could ship polished, consistent experiences without relying on heroics.

Case study · Enterprise banking

Enterprise banking: running design delivery across three banking platforms

At Canvs, I manage design delivery for a leading private-sector bank's mobile banking app, internet banking and digital onboarding journeys. That means a steady stream of feature requests, compliance changes and design reviews, handled by a multi-designer team against real release dates.

RoleProject Manager, UI/UX
ClientICICI Bank
PlatformsMobile, web & onboarding
Team8-person design team
Product screens are under NDA, so this case study shows the delivery work rather than the designs. Walkthroughs are available on request.
Scale

What the work looks like, in numbers

200mobile app requests tracked since April 2026
83%of those already delivered
3platforms running in parallel
50+Figma review threads with the client each month
The platforms

Three products, one delivery rhythm

Mobile banking appThe bank's flagship app and its new version: payments, accounts, cards, investments and service journeys, plus web versions of key flows.
Retail internet bankingThe new internet banking experience and updates to the live site, designed across desktop, tablet and mobile breakpoints.
Customer onboarding journeysDigital applications for loans, credit cards and accounts, from eligibility to KYC and e-sign.
Scope

The kinds of work we deliver

UPI & payments KYC & compliance Deposits & nominees Cards Loans Mutual funds & demat NRI banking Accessibility & design system Responsive breakpoints
How I run it

From client request to delivered design

Client request Notion tracker card Design in Figma Client review Build QA Delivered
One tracker per platformEvery request becomes a card with a type (main track, business-as-usual or support), priority, client owner, designer and target date.
Owners on both sidesEach card names a client owner and a Canvs designer, so nobody has to ask who's on it.
Feedback in one placeClient comments stay in Figma and are logged against the card, so revisions don't get lost in email.
QA before go-liveBuilds are checked against the design, and issues are raised before release.

Case study · Product I'm building

Throughline: design to delivery, in one thread

One workspace that runs a design-and-build project from brief to launch. Throughline reads Gmail, Figma, Notion and Drive, tells me what needs doing today, and turns the same data into reports my team and my client can each act on. I'm building it with Claude Cowork.

RoleProduct owner & builder
Built withClaude Cowork
Connects toGmail, Figma, Notion, Drive
StageOngoing
WORKSPACES3Overview, Design and Engineering, joined by one roadmap
VIEWS2Team and client, built from the same data
SOURCES4Gmail, Figma, Notion and Drive, read in place
TO ACT1 clickEvery alert arrives with its next step ready
The problem

Project work is scattered, so things slip between tools

Work lives in five placesBriefs arrive by email, feedback sits in Figma, tasks in Notion, files in Drive.
Client asks go missingA question in a Figma thread or an email is easy to forget until it's overdue.
Bottlenecks surface lateBlocked or overloaded work is usually spotted after a date has already moved.
Every update is written twiceOnce for the team with detail, and again in plain words for the client.
Why it's different

Built to move work forward, not just track it

Acts, not just tracks

Every alert comes with a ready next step, so spotting a problem and fixing it happen in the same place.

Works where work already happens

Reads Gmail, Figma, Notion and Drive directly. Nobody re-types updates into yet another tool.

Design and build, side by side

Each team gets its own home, tasks and report, joined by one shared roadmap.

Team and client in one workspace

Add both straight in. Each sees the version written for them, from the same source.

Plain words by default

Technical setup, risks and delays are explained so a non-technical client can follow.

Answers with receipts

Ask anything about the project and get an answer linked to the exact email or comment.

Inside the tool

Five parts, one thread

Screenshots are from the demo version, which runs on made-up sample data (a fictional bank called Kestrel). Select any screen to enlarge it.

Overview · plan, track, report

Overview: start every day knowing what matters

The command centre for the whole project, so I never have to open five tools to find out where things stand.

  • Today is an action inbox, not a to-do list. Every item arrives with its next step ready: a drafted reply, a nudge or a follow-up.
  • Brief in, plan out. Drop in a brief or meeting notes and the Project hub drafts scope, tasks, risks and tech setup for review.
  • A roadmap that updates itself, phase by phase from scoping to launch, with owners and progress against today.
Design · home, tasks, report

Design: every Figma comment closed, and shown to be closed

A home built for the design team, where client feedback is tracked until the client sees it resolved.

  • Feedback with a full loop: each Figma comment moves from assigned to done to shared back with the client.
  • Workload you can see: spots who has more work than time before a deadline moves.
  • Progress, bottlenecks and live Figma files on one screen.
Engineering · build, bugs, tech

Engineering: build progress anyone can follow

Its own home for developers and QA, joined to the same roadmap as design, so nothing falls between the two.

  • Tasks, bugs, blockers and phase progress together, with a clear on-track or at-risk status.
  • Log a bug or a task in one click; serious bugs are flagged before testing is signed off.
  • Tech setup in plain words: every technical choice explained so a non-technical client can follow.
Reporting · design and engineering

Reports: every bottleneck comes with the fix

Reports that tell you what to do next, not just what went wrong.

  • Separate design and engineering reports for the last 7, 14 or 30 days.
  • Impact and next step on every issue, from work waiting on the client to overloaded teammates.
  • A summary written by Claude, then export a PDF, copy it or email it in one step.
Sharing · team and client

Sharing: one workspace, two audiences

Everyone on the project lives in the same place, and each audience sees the version written for them.

  • Add teammates and clients straight to the workspace, each with a role, discipline and focus days that drive owners, workload and dates.
  • Team view keeps the detail: owners, workload, internal notes and one-click rebalancing.
  • Client view turns the same data into plain-language updates, ready to email to the client.
More screens

The details that make it work

My approach

From everyday friction to an automated workflow

Audit the workflow Prioritise pain points Automate the repetitive Refine through iteration
Workflow audit

Mapped a full delivery cycle across Gmail, Figma, Notion and Drive to see exactly where time, context and client requests were being lost.

Pain-point prioritisation

Ranked each issue by its impact on delivery. Missed client asks, late bottleneck detection and duplicated status reporting came first.

Automation-first design

Replaced manual follow-ups, status updates and report writing with review-ready drafts, while keeping a human decision on anything that reaches the client.

Continuous refinement

Refined each iteration against real delivery scenarios until every alert led to a clear action and every report read well for both team and client.
